title: An Interview With Camilla Crane, Librarian-in-Residence
content:
As a Librarian-in-Residence in the Library of Congress’s Web Archiving Section, Camilla Crane is exploring new ways to improve access to web archives. She discusses her path to web archiving, the challenges and surprises of preserving websites, and some of the internet “rabbit holes” she’s discovered along the way. 

Can you tell us a little about what you do as a Librarian-in-Residence at the Library of Congress? What are you working on, and what do you like most about your role? 

The Librarian-in-Residence (LIR) program gives early-career librarians the opportunity to develop their skills at the Library of Congress during a six-month appointment (with a possible four-month extension). I’m on the Digital Services track of the program, working in the Web Archiving Section (WA). I’ve been able to get involved in a variety of day-to-day operations managing the web archiving lifecycle, including quality assurance (QA) work and developing training materials for other Library divisions that interact with our collections.

title: AI Sandbox Series: The Embedded Catalog
content:
This post was written by Matthew Miller, a Linked Data Applications Technical Specialist in Discovery and Preservation Services at the Library of Congress. We are excited to share this post in our ongoing series about the Library of Congress Artificial Intelligence (AI) Sandbox for staff. Posts in the series will feature details about experiments in text recognition and searchability, metadata and bibliographic record enhancement, and more. A previous post introduced the initiative’s goals and an overview of the types of experiments conducted so far. 

Recently the staff of the Network Development and MARC Standards Office at the Library of Congress participated in an AI Sandbox program hosted by the Library’s Digital Strategy Directorate in the Office of the Chief Information Officer. The Sandbox provided a space to use AI and machine learning tools and methodologies with the Library’s collections and metadata at scale.

title: Preserving More Than the Web: Building an Archive of Online Resources for Preservation and Conservation
content:
In this interview, Jon Sweitzer-Lamme explains how web archiving is supporting the work of conservators and preservation scientists at the Library. He describes the process of creating the Preservation and Conservation Web Archive, what it preserves and why, the challenges of expanding the collection internationally, and how the archive can help future researchers understand the history of the field. 

What is your job at The Library of Congress and what was your role in creating this collection? 

I am a Preservation Librarian in the Conservation Division. Part of my role is ensuring that conservators and preservation scientists have access to the resources they need for their work, including new scholarly publications. As more of those resources became available only online, I realized we needed to preserve access for the future, which led to creating the Preservation and Conservation Web Archive. I am the Collection Leader, and I’ve researched the field and worked with colleagues across the Conservation Division to identify resources to include in the collection.

title: Become Part of the Legacy of Abolitionist and Educator, Myrtilla Miner
content:
Today’s post is from Lauren Algee, a Senior Digital Collections Specialist & By the People community manager at the Library of Congress. 

In 1851, more than a decade before the Emancipation Proclamation was issued, the School for Colored Girls opened in Washington, D.C. with the mission of training Black women educators. The institution was the first of its kind in the District and only the fourth in the nation. Today, the Library of Congress and the By the People volunteer transcription program invite you to celebrate the life and legacy of its courageous and barrier-breaking founder, Myrtilla Miner (1815-1864).

Miner spent her young adulthood teaching in New York, Rhode Island, and Mississippi. In the latter she was denied permission to conduct classes for enslaved children, after which she resolved to open her own school for “colored” women teachers. 

Frederick Douglass recalled that when she came to him asking for support for her endeavor, he “thought the proposition was reckless, almost to the point of madness” but “her resolution was taken, and was not to be shaken or changed.”

title: Anywhere Adventures in Southeast Wyoming
content:
The following is a guest post by the 2025-2026 Innovator in Residence, Vivian Li. As part of her work with the Library, Vivian hosted a series of community outreach events. Read on to learn about her time in Southeast Wyoming, one of the locations in Anywhere Adventures, Vivian’s mobile-first website which brings local history to users through comics and travel logs. 

At the beginning of July, I got to travel to Wyoming to do some in-person programming with our library collaborators in Cheyenne and Laramie!

In Cheyenne, because so many locations are within walking distance from the library, we did a walking tour of three Anywhere Adventures stops.

The first stop was at the Wyoming State Capitol building to see the statue of Esther Hobart Morris. Morris is known for being the first woman to hold public office as justice of the peace. We chose this first stop to ask some ice-breaker questions to get to know one another.  Participants had to choose one of the following difficult questions, and defend their answers:

  • If you could only eat one food for the rest of your life, what would it be?
  • What’s the ideal breakfast?
  • Are there more doors or wheels in the entire world?

title: The Zine Atlas
content:
The following is a guest post by the 2025-2026 Innovator in Residence, Vivian Li. As part of her work with the Library, Vivian hosted a series of community outreach events, including zine-making workshops in partnership with the Chicago Public Library. Read on to learn how you can also make a zine and check out the end of the post to print your own copy of research zines created by Vivan about various LOC collections.

In Chicago, the Anywhere Adventures team ran a series of workshops inviting people to make zines about their neighborhood. These zines could describe a piece of history that happened on your block, a memory you have, some kind of guide, or anything you want to share and preserve about your piece of the world.

I’ve been copying and gathering these zines into a community artbook called the Zine Atlas. If you would like to make a zine and contribute it to the Atlas, or if you just want to participate in the writing prompts we used in Chicago, you can do it yourself at home!

Materials needed:
– Paper (2 sheets)
– Scissors
– Drawing supplies (just a pencil/pen is fine, but feel free to use anything!)

title: Informing AI Strategy and Literacy: An Interview with Sylvia Staal Riordan
content:
In this interview, 2026 Library of Congress intern Sylvia Staal Riordan reflects on her experience working in the Digital Strategy Directorate of the Library’s Office of the Chief Information Officer. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Leah: Hi Sylvia! It’s great to have you on our team this summer. Could you tell us about your role at the Library, and what you’ve worked on?

Sylvia: My role at the Library this summer was Artificial Intelligence Community Specialist Intern, which involved working with the Digital Strategy Directorate on various AI literacy, strategy, and community engagement initiatives.

One of the main AI literacy projects I completed was taking the Library’s Principles for Responsible AI Use and mapping them to actionable AI-related competencies. I shared this in a chart format that was easily readable and accessible for Library staff members regardless of their familiarity with AI, hopefully to help empower them to make informed judgements about the technology. I also conducted a survey with my fellow interns to gauge their feelings about AI to help inform the direction of AI literacy at the Library, and was involved with AI strategy development.

title: Web Archive Collections in Online Reference Resources
content: It’s officially fall, and in the U.S. that means the new school year is in full swing with bus stops, backpacks, books, and best friends. As primary source literacy and digital literacy become more critical than ever for elementary through higher education students, initiatives like the Library’s By the People and the National Archives and Records Administration’s Citizen Archivist Program bring historical documents right to desktops for transcription projects. Thanks to projects like these, teaching with primary sources and learning directly from them have never been easier. But have you ever thought about web archives in the context of these back-to-school materials? If not, let’s change that! Archived websites are born-digital primary sources of our current age that offer a plethora of information literacy opportunities for educators and students alike.

title: Founding Documents in Context: AI-Powered and Grounded Cultural Heritage
content:
This post describes a recent collaboration between the Digital Strategy Directorate in the Library’s Office of the Chief Information Officer and the Arizona State University Cloud Innovation Center. The partnership explored necessary steps to create an effective AI-powered tool using context engineering that allows for the exploration of United States Revolutionary Era history with the Library’s collections as grounding data.

As opportunities to discover uncharted patterns in our nation’s history expand with artificial intelligence-powered research tools, technical approaches that promote authenticity and context are needed more than ever.

Recently, the Library’s Digital Strategy Directorate teamed up with Arizona State University Cloud Innovation Center students to investigate how technical innovation can be grounded in truth using founding era documents.

title: New Online at the Library of Congress: September 2026
content:
Interested in learning more about what’s new in the Library of Congress’s digital collections? The Signal shares regular updates and we love showing off our colleagues’ hard work from across the Library. Read on for a sample of recent additions and a few favorite highlights. Click here for all previous updates.

A Thank You From Us 

Thanks to everyone who came out to The Library of Congress National Book Festival in August! “New Online at the Library of Congress” newsletter contributors engaged with hundreds of attendees about virtual volunteering, web archiving, and Library of Congress digital collections. We hope to see you again next year! In the meantime, we hope you’ll enjoy learning about the latest additions to the Library’s digital collections: 

The Law Library of Congress Records and Briefs collection consists of the briefs and transcripts of records submitted to the Supreme Court of the United States on appeal from federal courts and state appellate courts. This initial release includes nearly 10,000 documents from 3,000 cases spanning the years 1999-2013. The collection offers full-text searching as well as metadata including case name, U.S. Reports citation, and file date.
